utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies, Mr. Krasniqi. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krasniqi. Yesterday, you told us that having crossed --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- the border into Albania, you went to the town of Kukes where you received some medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to show you a couple clips from a video that depicts you while you were in Kukes with your injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we, Your Honour, move on to play a clip from the video with the number 02343.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "UNKNOWN SPEAKER: Today is the 4th of April, 1999. The time is ten to 8.00 in the evening. We are here at Kukes with the witness, Mehmed Avdyli. He is a witness that comes from Kosovo, from the village of Krusa e Vogel. He sustained -- allegedly sustained these injuries, burn injuries from being put into a house by Serb policemen, and eventually surviving the attack where 110 people perished. They were shot and burned to death. We are now in a position to place the injuries on video tape for further evidence. Can you tell me what your name is? "MEHMED AVDYLI: Mehmet Avdyli. "UNKNOWN VOICE: And where do you come from? "MEHMED AVDYLI: Krusha e Vogel, [indiscernible]."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. With your leave, Your Honour, may I move on to clip 2, which I think is shorter than clip 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is a video of the 4th of April showing the burn injuries on your face and your hands. The person who was speaking on the video referred to 110 men who were killed in Krusha e Vogel. I'd like to ask you this first. Do you recall on that day giving a statement to the investigators of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I indicated yesterday, the statement is part of P 2341, which I don't propose to tender the entire statement into evidence but just the part that I want to use to refresh his memory as to who the men were. So with your leave, Your Honour, I think the best way to go through with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have the witness look at the statement. There's a good starting point, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to have the English version which he signed, as the customary situation, on the screen for Your Honours, and I hand him the Albanian interpretation as well as a copy of the English version, so he could have a look at those while Your Honours have the benefit of seeing the copy, signed copy in English. If I could proceed that with your leave, Your Honour. Mr. Usher, could I hand to you these two. May I indicate to my friends for the Defence that the B/C/S copy of this statement is at page 10 of the e-court B/C/S translation of the statement. This is page 1, this is English, and I think for Mr. Djordjevic you could give him a copy of the B/C/S. I was just reminded, Your Honours, may I tender those two video-clips and accept them, received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00303, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You could have a look through that document before you, Mr. Krasniqi. That's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Usher. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, please -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is P2341, and I'd like you to take us straight to page 10 of the English in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to come up on the screen, Mr. Krasniqi, you could look at the signed document on your right. You could look at the various pages to see where you have signed.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It seems -- while we are waiting for that to come up on the screen, Your Honours, may I press along and then return to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you eventually reunited with your family, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where had they gone to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had gone to a village close to Berat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Berat is in which country?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Albania, in the southern part of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in what sort of condition were they living in that village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very good conditions, of course. It was not our home. They were refugees, all of them. When they saw me, however, because they had heard that I had died, when they saw me that appeared there alive, they were very, very happy. They were very happy that I had survived the massacre.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... enter in some printed version since on the -- electronic system is not up this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, after -- I'll withdraw it. May I put it this way, did you sat some point return to Krusha e Vogel with your family?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back on the 26th of June together with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the various -- the several men, 110 we're told in that video, who were in the barn with you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see any of them again?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember who you saw? How many survived from the barn, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went back to Krusha e Vogel, I saw that five other people had survived: Lutfi Ramadani, Agim Asllani, Qamil Shehu, Bajram Zylfiu, and Petrit Rashkaj. All five had survived the massacre as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The remaining men numbering over 100, did you ever see them again?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you're from that village, you know their family and their relatives. Do you know if their family and their relatives ever saw them again?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go and have a look at the house and the barn where the execution took place?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went together with my family, and all the people went there to see. About every five minutes, people would come to see what had happened there, what was left there. They couldn't find anything, just some bones and a pair of shoes that were burned, and also, the wheelchair of Sait Hajdari, who was disabled, because they had taken away everything, and they had blown up the place, both rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to tell us, just what do you mean by "they had taken away everything"? What had they taken away?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house was not there. The ashes were not there -- were not there. Everything had been cleaned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you say the place had the been blown up, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had mined the place. Both rooms were now holes. The foundations, everything, the walls, everything had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where did you see the bones and the shoes?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the villagers who had come earlier before me to Krusha e Vogel had collected those things and had put them on the side of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, could I show to the witness 00100. That's 65 ter 00100. These are photos of the area that the witness just described taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, there might be problems with the -- well, let's see if this one comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What does this photograph before you depict, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This picture shows the place that had been cleaned up and blown up. Both rooms had been mined, and because of the explosion, my uncle's house was damaged as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is your uncle's house the red brick structure to the left of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And about where on this photograph would the house where the massacre took place be?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this one. There was just 1-metre difference between the two houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So on this photograph, can you see the place where the destroyed house was?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see some foundations here in front, but the grasses and the vegetation have covered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to photo number 2 on that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is the same place, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Photo number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that the same place?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we just scroll through fairly quickly the remaining four or five photos because they depict the same thing, the same area. Stop at this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is that -- and it's on this one. What is that hole we see there with water in it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These two places full of water are the places that were blown up. Even today you can find water in those two craters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you just continue to the end of this album. Your Honour, could the album received in evidence and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00304, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How many photographs are there altogether?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nine, Your Honour. Perhaps I should do a count. Ten -- nine photographs plus the cover page, so the exhibit is ten pages, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nine photographs is the exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could return, with your leave, Your Honours, to P2341. Sorry. 002341. And I'm corrected again. It's 02341. And if we could move straight to page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On that first page of the document, Mr. Krasniqi, I think you said that you had signed it. You see your name there, though, is -- you signed it "Avdyli."

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was before your name change.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on to page 13 on e-court, and that's Albanian page 15, Albanian translation page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You'll see that you say in this statement, and I'll read it, I think you can see it in your own language, as well, to the right --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that to the right is the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have an Albanian copy in front of you, translation. Yes, you can open it. If you can, find where the list of names begin. And you said that: "I am now a refugee in Albania and have elected to make this statement to the war crimes Tribunal. The following persons whose names I know and approximate ages were taken into the rooms and executed." And you see the names you have listed. I think you have listed the names on the -- the families of the persons. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'd like you to just look through it right to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could on e-court move to the English page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the end where you see again you have signed it at the end there.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to this list, to the first page of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is English page 13 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see in the Batusha family, you have mentioned -- you have Sefer, age 19 there. Do you see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefer Batusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you find out anything about him after you gave this list?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to Albania, I didn't know then that he wasn't in the village. That's why I mentioned him here. I mentioned several persons that were not in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, was he -- is he alive or dead? Did you discover whether he's alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is still living. He was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you look under the -- just further down, under the Ramadani family, you see Lufti, age 58. After you gave this list, did you discover whether or not Lufti is alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Lutfi Ramadani, I thought he was dead. I didn't know that he survived the massacre. After some time in Albania, I heard that Lutfi Ramadani, Bajram Zylfiu, Petrit Rashkaj, Agim Asllani, and Xhemajl Shehu had also survived the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move to the next page, you see under the Hajdari family, you see Hysni, age 20, "was apparently shot in the forest after escaping."

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was shot in the mountains, in the forest. I found him dead there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say "after escaping." After escaping from where?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After escaping the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, apart from those two persons that you said survived, were on this list, are the remainder of the persons on this list dead or alive, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are all dead, the remaining persons on the list. Only 20 bodies were identified and buried in our village. The remaining victims, we don't know where they are. We never found their remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Stamp, that we have not been able to follow this clearly. It would be, I believe, desirable for you to take the witness to the names of each one of those whom he now says survived as those names appear on this list. The problem is principally that he is -- after you took you to one member of the Batusha family --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- and you moved then to a Ramadani family member, after that there was no identification of the individuals with the list. The people recording the transcript have made their best effort trying to record the names, but they are quite different from the recording that's in the list, as far as I can see. So if we're going to make any use of this, we will need to have specific identification of the survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see on the transcript, Mr. Krasniqi --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- that you named some of the persons -- or the persons who survived the massacre, or who escaped from the building. Can you name them again, very slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Each one needs to be identified with a name on the list, if I can suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just want to get the names first because not all of them were put on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just name those survivors that you know of, very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lutfi Ramadani, Agim Asllani, Bajram Zylfiu, Petrit Rashkaj, Xhemajl Shehu.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you had pointed us to Lufti Ramadani, and that is at English page 13 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lutfi Ramadani also survived the massacre. His two sons were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we perhaps proceed this way. Under the family name "Batusha," Sefer is listed age 19. I think the witness has now made it clear that that person he now understands had survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When we come to the Ramadani family, there is listed a Lutfi, whereas the witness is recorded in the transcript has speaking of a Lufti. Probably they're the same person. Can that be clarified? Aged 58 is the indication in the list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Lutfi. It's the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, is there also in your understanding, did Bajram Ramadani survive or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bajram Ramadani did not survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Asllani family, you mentioned one of those who you now believe survived. Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Agim Asllani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I don't identify such a name on the list. I have Adem, and I have an Asim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just ask you this: Did you include on the list all the persons who escaped from the house where the execution took place, or did you only include Sefer and Lutfi? That is Sefer Batusha and Lutfi Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Agim was there when the massacre occurred and that he survived, that he left the location of the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you did not -- if you look at the list, you did not include him on the list at the time.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I guess I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Bajram, and I'm sure I'll get the pronunciation wrong, Bajram Zylfiu. He --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bajram Zylfiu also survived the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you will see on the last page of list, you did not include him on the list of those killed.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you will see at the end of the list --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 15 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You could just follow us on the B/C/S copy you have there. You say the other three survivors are Agim Asllani, whom I have been told is alive, Petrit Rashkaj, and Bajram Zylfiu.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So we can see that of the survivors on this list, only Sefer Batusha and Lutfi Ramadani you mentioned as being alive?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at Kukes, I didn't know that he had survived the massacre. He came to Albania very, very late. As for Sefer Batusha, I didn't know at the time that he was not in the village. He had been in Germany at the time, but that I didn't know. So that's why I mentioned these names because I thought that they were in the village at the time, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if that clarified it, Your Honour. You see that there are five survivors. He had named two in his list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are five survivors as well as himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Six, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he had named two in his list, which he subsequently discovered were alive, and he mentioned that there were three others at the end of the list. So as I say, not all the survivors were included in the list, just two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Of the list two that are listed, namely Sefer Batusha and Lutfi Ramadani, are now believed by the witness to have survived, as I understand it, and in addition to himself, the three other people whom he had not put on the list are known by him now to have been old but have survived. They are Agim Asllani, Petrit Rashkaj, and Bajram Zylfiu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, if those names are correct, we also have mentioned in the transcript yet one further name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I am the one who contributed to this state of confusion because there should be two other persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can understand by now, Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- the cause of our concern when I first intervened. We do not presently know clearly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, who the survivors are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- who are the names on this list who are now thought by the witness to have survived, and who are the people he now believes survived but who he did not put on the list. Now, Qamil Shehu, is he a person who the witness believes to have survived or not? Perhaps the witness might be able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Qamil Shehu survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that appears to be, then, number 6 in addition to the witness, which would suggest seven survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefer Batusha is not a survivor of the massacre. He at the time was in Germany, but I personally made a mistake, mentioned his name on the list because I had no knowledge that he was not there in the village at the critical time. However, survivors are the following: Qamil Shehu, Lutfi Ramadani, Agim Asllani, Petrit Rashkaj, and Bajram Zylfiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And yourself?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those were the persons who were in the building who manage to escape alive?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go back to the list, and I'm afraid I might cause even a little bit more complexity. If you look at the Avdyli and Batusha family at the beginning of the list, you will see Muharrem, 69, and his nephew. Was his nephew in the house or the barn where the execution took place?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you look on the last page of the list, under the Shehu family, I think in Albanian that is the page before the last, but you need to find the Shehu family. You see near to the bottom of the list, son of Sinan, 18. Was he in the house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the only thing I can do is to ask you, as having looked at the list, apart from those that are mentioned and that -- or that you have mentioned, actually, did anyone else survive?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those that we mentioned and whose names are on the list and who survived the massacre are Agim Asllani, myself, Bajram Zylfiu, Lutfi Ramadani, and Petrit Rashkaj. Sefer Batusha and Muharrem's nephew, Sinan's son, they were not survivors because they were not there where the massacre occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I hope, Your Honour, that that clarifies the situation with this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we are now in a clearer position, Mr. Stamp, and you propose now to tender the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would not propose to tender the entire statement because he has given evidence as to the narrative in the statement, but perhaps the sentence which I'll just read: "The following persons whose names I know and approximate ages were taken into the rooms and executed." If from that part to the sentence immediately after the end of the list, which I will now read: "The other three survivors are Agim Asllani, whom I have been told is alive, and Petrit Rashkaj, and Bajram Zylfiu. I have only seen Petrit at Kukes." If that section could be just severed from the statement and received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The list of survivors that, part of the statement will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we do -- I'm wondering if we could just have the -- at least the last sentence, the sentence immediately after the list because that helps clarify the evidence, and the sentence immediately before as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we have now the oral evidence of the witness. Once it was eventually clarified, we know what he says about various people who are either wrongly listed or who have been omitted from the list and are known to have survived, and we know which of those on the list he says he now thinks survived. Why do we want yet another version of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I guess -- Your Honour, I guess -- I think I'm just being more cautious, possibly more than necessary. The list, in agreement with the Court, in addition to his evidence, is sufficient, but I just think it's just a little bit more clear if those two sentences are included. [Trial Chamber confers

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The exhibit will include the paragraph that introduces the list, commencing: "I am now a refugee in Albania ..." and the paragraph that is at the immediate end of the list: "The other three survivors are Agim Asllani ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Am I correct in thinking it was a list in its original form of 96 names?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think I am -- because of the way the list is constructed, at some parts he says, for example, if you look at the beginning, he might say in respect to the Batushas, Zaim, 50, and two sons, Feim, 23, and other's name is unknown, 20. That's two of his sons. There are occasions where each line represents more than one person, so the list comes to a total of 100 names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But I will, ask Your Honour, if at the end of the next break I could give the total in respect to -- the total minus those that he says survived because I did a count yesterday, and I'd like to just confirm it just to be absolutely accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you'd better because with your having pointed out how some listings are in fact of two or even three people, I make the list to include over 100 names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I had 102 minus 2, but I could -- I would like to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We won't waste time now, but can I say I was at 104 on the last count.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we will get that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, do you have cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some technical problems, and I will find another earphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Krasniqi. I am Defence counsel for the accused in this case. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic, and I will ask you some questions that I believe if answered will help clarify the facts in this case. Mr. Krasniqi, can you tell us, what was your surname when you were born?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was born, my surname was Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, when did you change your birth surname, Krasniqi, to Avdyli?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly how many years after I was born. My uncle changed it to Avdyli. That's the surname my grandfather had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your uncle, is he your maternal or paternal uncle? Which grandfather are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My uncle, my father's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the grandfather?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father's brother. My grandfather was my father's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why the surname "Krasniqi" was changed into Avdyli? Why did your uncle change your surname and his own surname into Avdyli?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he changed that. He uses the surname "Avdyli" himself while myself and my brothers use the surname "Krasniqi."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you said that your paternal grandfather was called Avdyli?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My grandfather was called Avdyli.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did your father also bear the surname "Avdyli"?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May I then conclude that your father's surname was Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you bear the surname "Avdyli"? You can't explain this to the Court and you can't tell the Trial Chamber because your father's surname was Krasniqi; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went to school, I went to school together with his children, and he came and changed his son's surname and my surname, so all the surnames in the school figured as Avdyli.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you live in your uncle's family?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't live in my uncle's house. We were together, all of us living together; my father, my uncles were living together until 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I can't understand whether you are the son of Avdyli or the son of Krasniqi because your father is Krasniqi, and we see that your surname currently is Krasniqi as well.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when we went to school, he changed the surname. I didn't know that he had changed the surname those days from Krasniqi to Avdyli. He was a little authoritative, and that's why I did not change the surname until lately. When I was grown up and changed the surname just like my brothers, I became a Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen? When did you change your surname to Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: One more question about your surname. You say your uncle changed his name to Avdyli and you didn't know about that for a long time. When did you become aware of that, that you were in fact Avdyli by surname, not Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was at school, I learned that he had changed the surname into Avdyli. I was a young boy at the time. That was my uncle, my eldest uncle. I was scared. I didn't tell anyone, so the surname remained Avdyli until I changed it to Krasniqi again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about a portion of the list that was shown to us a few minutes ago and part of which has been admitted into evidence. It's the list of people who were allegedly in the building that caught fire and where the massacre was perpetrated. Can you explain to me that since you and your brothers are all Krasniqi, there is not a single Krasniqi on this list? We see Avdyli but not a single Krasniqi. Do the Krasniqis live in Krusha e Vogel at all?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do. At that time during the war, we were living separately. We were separated. Some of us were on the main road, and they were told together with their families to go to the Duni [as interpreted] river, while the others were told to go to the forest. I was the only one in the second group that was told to go to the forest, and my uncle, as well, Bali Avdyli and Enver Avdyli, they were close to me; their houses were close to mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Krasniqi, you say they told us to go to the forest and they told them to go to the river. Who told to you go to the forest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Serb forces came, the people in the village -- all the people in the village who were living on the upper side of the road were told to go to the mountains, to the forest, and when I saw that all the people were going towards the forest, I went together with them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But my question was, Who told them to go to the forest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me personally, but I went together with other people who were going to the forest. Somebody had told them, the Serbs, the soldiers or the policemen who were there. I did not see them myself, but the people who were closest to the road must have been told, and when I saw the people going towards the forest, I joined the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you these questions because you just said that they were told to go to the forest and to the river respectively. Do you suppose somebody told them, or is it based on some certain knowledge, because you are mentioning it for the first time today. So do you suppose somebody told them - because you told us somebody told them - or you have reliable information about this?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from other people. The forces had told them. The police and military forces had told them to go to the forest, the one who lived on the upper part of the village, while those on the lower part of the village were told to go towards Drin, and I heard this from the villagers, that they had been told to go towards the forest, and I joined the group and went to the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this again because we understood something different yesterday -- earlier today. Early in that morning, you said you went to the forest, but I want to ask you, since you heard from other people that it was the Serb forces or the Serb police, as you now specify, I want to ask you, did those people also tell you the reason why they were told to go to the forest and why the other group that lived lower down in the village was told to go to the river? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the reason why they told half of the villagers to go to the forest and the others to go towards the river. I don't know the reason. What I know is that we were set on fire, we were massacred, we were burned, and that must be the reason, that -- what they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Krasniqi. You talked about that yesterday, and we'll discuss it at a later stage when the time comes in my cross-examination, but to save time and out of respect for everyone in the courtroom, I am asking you again to answer my questions directly. Why are you saying this for the first time? Why haven't you said this ever before; namely, that somebody from the police, from the Serbs, told the villagers to go towards the forest or towards the Drin river, to leave their homes? Why haven't you ever mentioned this before, and it's important, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Do you have brothers or sisters?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How many brothers and how many sisters?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two brothers, two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, did any of your brothers belong to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many members are there to the Krasniqi family? When I say Krasniqi, I mean the family that should bear that surname by your father. Are you now called Krasniqi, all of you, you and your brothers? I'm not going to ask about the sisters if they are married.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I hear you from interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are 15 members in our family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely my next question. On the list of these people you say were executed in their house on the 26th of March, 1999, and you made that list while being interviewed by the Prosecution on the 4th of April, 1999, while you were giving the statement, and on that list there is not a single Krasniqi. It is clear why now, but it's also clear that the members of your closest family are Avdyli. Is Bali Avdyli 72 years old and Enver Avdyli 28 years old? Are they members of your family?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bali Avdyli is my uncle. Enver Avdyli is his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. You told us yesterday that on the 25th of March, Serb forces came and surrounded the village coming from the main road, Prizren-Djakovica, and that the people were concerned, worried, and that's why they went into the mountains. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that yesterday because the first people that I met when I went out and I asked them where they were going, they said the Serbian forces had come and surrounded us. Some of them told me that somebody had shouted, Go to the mountain, go to the mountain. Some of them shouted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, did you also say yesterday that you personally saw these people coming, I mean the Serb forces, that they had all sorts of combat vehicles, tanks, armoured vehicles, APCs, heavy artillery, and that you saw all that with your own eyes; or is it something as you say today that some people who were going to the forest told you? Which of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see the forces myself, and I heard them when they were coming towards the village. The whole village roared, and I saw them myself when they were going on the road and stopped opposite the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you stated yesterday that it happened almost at dawn, at 5.00 a.m. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had not dawned yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the legal officer to call up D001-4180, page 2 in English, and alongside this document to display D001-4196, page 2, paragraph 4, in Albanian. Thank you. But we are seeing something else. It's not the -- so page 2 of both documents, both the English and the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I want to discuss is on page 2 in English, paragraph 4, and page 2, paragraph 4, in Albanian. The Prosecutor has provided you with a hard copy. You have it before you. Check page 2. You say: "The next morning, 25th March, 1999, I was awakened by the noise of the tanks in the village. It was about 3 a.m., and the tanks were close to the houses. I woke up my wife and told her to leave with the children and hide in the mountains. I left for the forest with my family, and all the other Albanian families did the same." Mr. Krasniqi, there is a significant discrepancy in the hour. You will admit that 3.00 a.m. and 5.00 a.m. is not the same thing. Why when your memory was much fresher did you say that it was at 3.00 a.m., and today you are saying it was 5.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about 3.40. In one of my statements I gave, I mentioned 3.40, and I'm very sure about that. At that time, we heard the noise. I looked outside and saw the forces coming towards the village from the direction of the road, main road, Prizren-Gjakove, when they came to the village. It was about 5.00 a.m. when I left the house together with the children and my wife, and we joined the group of people leaving. I asked some of them, Where are you going? And they told me -- some of them were telling me that they had been told to go to the mountain, and some of them who had want to go towards the river had been stopped and told to go towards the forest, and that was the group that I joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time we're hearing this from you. I've said this often enough, and I won't repeat it, but before we go on a break, I'll just ask you if you signed this statement or not, the statement that is before you on the screen and the hard copies on your desk.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suppose it's a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us continue, Mr. Krasniqi. Mr. Krasniqi, yesterday during the direct examination, you said that you did not see what the policemen, the Serb forces, whoever, were doing and what they were doing in the village, but you said: We could hear fire from pistols, and we could only see smoke from houses. Do you agree that that's what you stated yesterday, page 66, lines 19, 20, and 21, yesterday's daily transcript? I'm saying this for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and my colleagues from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When my colleague Mr. Stamp asked you whether anything else happened on the 25th, you said that nothing had happened, that there was only shooting from pistols, and you said that you could see tree branches falling because of the bullets and that apart from that, nothing else happened. That's what you stated yesterday as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, in putting what the witness had said yesterday to him said that he heard the sound of pistols, fire from pistols. We have no recollection of pistols being mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that the English word "pistol" means "pistolj." There are other words, too, but there is this English word "gun" as well, and I wanted to clarify in my next question whether it is actually gun-fire coming from guns or whether it is fire coming from pistols. It was precisely for that reason that I wanted to clarify this. It's the daily transcript, the one from yesterday, actually, page 66, paragraphs 19, 20, and 21, and then what I asked continues in 24, 25, 26, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So, was this gun-fire coming from guns or rifles or firing coming from pistols? Because in English, this may be ambiguous -- an ambiguous word when it is used, "gun," that is.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the direction of the main road, I couldn't see from what kind of weapons they were firing, but the shooting, the gun-fire was directed at the forest. It couldn't have been gun-fire from a pistol or rifle because the forces that took up positions around the village, they had APCs and other heavy machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now it's clear. Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Could we have this same transcript on the monitor again, the one that was here until a few moments ago. I don't know if it's still there. D001-4080 in English, and in Albanian, D001-4916. It is page 2, paragraph 4. That is exactly where we were, so it's the same thing. Now, you said in that statement, the statement of the 4th of April, 1999, have a look at paragraph 4, please. When it dawned, tanks started firing at the upper part of the forest. The firing went on for a while, and then they started torching the village. Can you explain the difference between your statement on the 4th of April, 1999, what I referred to just now, and could you tell us why you stated that then and why you're saying something completely different now.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention every vehicle by name, whether it was an APC or a tank. I said that these were forces. They had heavy machinery with them. They did not fire from pistols or rifles. They were firing from these heavy machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that now you've totally confused me, Mr. Krasniqi. Yesterday and today, all of us in this courtroom understood that there was fire coming possibly from rifles, perhaps pistols, and now you're talking about shelling. Could you kindly clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to interrupt, but your impression of the evidence yesterday differs from others'. There was no understanding at all of pistols. What was described simply was gun-fire, and the witness yesterday went on to describe how branches of trees were being shot off, which in my mind was suggesting the firing of heavy weapons or heavy automatic weapons. He didn't specify that, but he described the effect of it. So that I think when you were suggesting to him now that he -- what you heard yesterday suggested pistols or rifles, that that is not the impression shared by others of what the witness was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then I would kindly ask that we all look at the daily transcript, page 66, paragraphs 19, 20, and 21. Could that please be displayed on our screens, the daily transcript, and what is written there is: "However, we could hear firing from ..." something that is called "guns" in English, "... and we could see smoke coming from the houses." It doesn't say "shelling." It says "shooting or firing." In this statement that I presented to the witness just now from the 4th of April, he says that it was tanks that were shelling the forest, in actual fact, and you will admit that this is a significant difference, namely between what the witness said on the 4th of April and what he said yesterday and what he's saying today. That is why I put my question. It has nothing to do with my impression. It is quite simply the situation as the exhibits stand, and that is why I'm putting this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, let me make it clear to you, Mr. Djordjevic, that from my understanding of the evidence yesterday, there is no significant difference between what the witness said in his original statement and what he was describing yesterday. The only possible uncertainty from yesterday arises because the witness was not specifically asked whether it was the armoured vehicles that were firing or some other type of fire, but what he did describe was gun-fire and the effect of the firing on the vegetation, and that seems to be quite inconsistent with simply the firing of small arms, whether it's pistols or rifles. It's consistent with the firing of heavier weapons, which is exactly what he was saying in his original statement. So please understand that your interpretation may not be shared by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. It is for the Court to draw its conclusions at the end. The parties certainly cannot do that. We can make our proposals and we can try to present what we want to present, so I fully abide by that, and everyone can have his or her own views, and he don't have to be identical. I will accept what you said by way of a remark, but my understanding of the transcript was quite different. Now I'm going to put a direct question to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Whether there was any shelling of your positions by the Serb forces while you were in the forest. So this is my direct question, whether the tanks fired at the forest where you had gone, as you had put it, upon instructions received by some people coming from elsewhere, as you had put it.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was shelling from the machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to put one more question to you. Now you say there was shelling from the machinery. That is what the interpretation I heard says. I must admit to you that I don't understand what this word "machinery" means, so I would like to clarify the matter fully.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military machinery. I heard the gun-fire coming from this heavy machinery. We saw the branches falling on ground as a result of being hit by this machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to be very specific. Were the branches falling because they had been hit, or were they falling due to an explosion?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They fall because they were hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now it is much clearer. My next question, Mr. Krasniqi, at that point in time were any of the villagers hurt due to the firing from the military machinery, as you had put it, in the forest on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Now everything is much clearer to me, at least, if not to all in the courtroom. Your house and the yard of Sejdi Batusha, yesterday you said that you stayed in the forest until the following morning and that those who had young children went to Sejdi Batusha's house while you remained in the forest. That is in the daily transcript, page 67, paragraphs 8, 9, and 10. Your statement from the 27th of June that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal in 2001, D001/ --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot follow the numbers, very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask to admit into evidence parts of the transcript from the 4th of April, 19 -- just a moment, please. What I said a few minutes ago, let me give you an accurate number so there is no misunderstanding. So there was D001, D -- or, rather, D001 -- just a moment, please, in order to be as specific as possible. Here it is. The 4th of April, 1999, D001-4180, page 2, paragraph 4, in English; and D001-4196, page 2, paragraph 4, in the Albanian. That is the part of the transcript that I would like to have admitted into evidence before I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The better procedure, Mr. Djordjevic, would be for you to put what it is that you want to put from that previous statement to the witness. If you want to draw our attention to some change from what is in the statement to what is being said now, do that, and at the end of that process the Chamber will then be able to decide whether the original statement should be admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. The only thing missing is my explanation as to why I believe this should be done. I believe that this should be done because we heard that the witness said that tanks were firing at the forest. In actual fact, it is obvious that there weren't any explosions; rather, the branches were falling off the trees because they had been hit, not due to explosions. Therefore, we may conclude that this is fire coming from some lighter weapons that are firing at the forest, and that is why I wanted this part of the transcript to be admitted into evidence. That is why the Defence is tendering that, and I have already put that to the witness as you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What you haven't put to the witness, Mr. Djordjevic, is whether what he has now said in evidence is different from what he said in his statement about this firing. I'm afraid the picture is becoming more and more confused by the questions rather than clearer. So if it is that you're saying the witness has changed his account from what he said in his statement to what he gave in evidence, you need to put to him specifically what you say the change is and have him comment upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've already done that. You can see that in the transcript, but I will do it yet again. Statement to the investigators of the Tribunal, the 4th of April, 1999. The English version is D001-4180, page 2, paragraph 4. The Albanian version is D001-4196, page 2, paragraph 4. The witness says: "When it dawned, the tanks started firing into the upper part of the forest. The shooting lasted for about one hour, and then they started to burn down the village." I just asked the witness whether there was any shelling, whether there were any explosions heard. The witness today said "no." He said branches were falling not because there were explosions but because they were hit. That is the difference between the statement that he gave then and the one that he gave now, nothing else. Of course, if the Court believes that this should not be admitted into evidence, I will accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely accurate, I don't think the witness said that there were no explosions. I think the witness said that the branches were not falling because of explosions. There's a slight difference and possibly an important difference if this issue is an important issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: When did the witness say this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness said at line 30 -- at page 31 today; line 20, the question was: "I have to be specific. Were the branches falling because they had been hit, or were they falling due to an explosion? "A. They fall because they were hit." So what I'm saying is the witness did not say there were no explosions. He said the branches fell because they were hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber has the difficulty, Mr. Djordjevic, that it doesn't see what you see in this evidence. We have read -- listened to your quote from the original statement where the witness simply says: "When it started to become light, these tanks fired in the upper part of the forest. The shooting lasted about one hour ..." The witness has described in his evidence that they were shooting. We've gone through the question whether he could say what was being shot. Pistols and rifles were put to him and he said, No, this was shooting from the military machinery, and he has described both tanks and armoured personnel carriers, both of which are armed with heavier weaponry. And then this question was, Was there shooting into the forest, and it was clear that it was. And the question then was, Whether branches were being -- falling from trees because of explosions or because of a more direct impact of whatever was being fired, and he said, It was not an explosion, they were being hit directly. At the moment, the evidence doesn't suggest to us firing from anything but what he described as the military machinery, and that, as you will know, could be either the cannons of tanks or the heavy machine guns fitted to armoured personnel carriers, and where we can see in all of that a difference from what is originally said to here is something that doesn't impress itself upon me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will agree with you, Your Honour, that it is possible that the fire was coming from the APCs or from the tanks but only from lighter weapons, small-caliber ones. However, in order for us to know whether tanks were firing from their cannons, I believe we would need a military expert because when cannons of tanks fire, there are also explosions involved. Where the shell ends up, it explodes. So let me be allowed to continue, and I hope that the situation will be clearer ultimately. Could we now have on our monitors the following document, a hand-written statement made by Mr. Krasniqi at the Orahovac police station in the summer of 1999. The English version is D001-5950, page 2, paragraph 1. I cannot give an exact reference for the Albanian version because it doesn't really exist. That is an annex to this document, to the version that was compiled in English, but it is paragraph 4 -- page 4, rather, paragraph 1, where we're talking about the Albanian language. I think that it would be useful so that the witness himself could see it. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krasniqi, do you see this statement of yours? Is this actually your statement? Let me ask you that first.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In this part of your written statement, at the place that I refer to earlier on, you say, In the morning, shelling started and houses in the village started burning. My first question: Shelling started. Can we conclude that the shelling started and that the fire was directed at the village and that is why the houses were burning, or is it something else that we are going to hear from you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the word "shelling," you can interpret it in whichever way you like. These -- the gun-fire came from the forces. I was not specific. I did not mention by names the equipment and the weapons. It was shelling coming from military machinery. This is what I meant by shelling, something coming from the military machinery, gun-fire coming from military machinery. As for houses burning, there was flames and smoke coming out from the houses. I don't know how these -- how these -- how the fire -- these houses were set on fire, but there was smoke and flames coming out of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying, Mr. Krasniqi, to find out from you, this shelling that morning, did you hear without seeing where these shells were landing, because we all know what happens when a shell hits the ground; or you know what the shells were targeting, or alternatively, you only heard shelling, that is, the sound of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the shelling. However, I did not see where the projectiles were falling. I just saw the branches of the trees falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Were the positions where the civilians from Mala Krusa hid in the forest shelled?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. We were in the forest, but no one was injured. The shelling went beyond where we were staying, up in the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think by now it's completely clear what happened. Mr. Krasniqi, would you tell me whether at that time, the time of the massacre, as you call it, you were aware what the Kosovo Liberation Army was, what kind of organisation it was and what's the purpose it served?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the KLA, I had heard, all of us had heard about it; however, I never saw them. I never joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, does that mean that you are claiming that the KLA was not familiar to you at all, that you knew no one from that organisation, you didn't know a single villager who joined the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw anyone in uniform from the KLA. I never stayed with them. Of course, I stayed with people, but I didn't know whether they were from the KLA or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask a part of the transcript to be shown of the 5th October, 2001. It's a statement of this witness given to the investigators of the Tribunal. It's D001-4218, page 2, please, paragraph 2. And in Albanian, it's D001-4226, page 2, paragraphs 2 and 3. We see that on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Look at your own statement, Mr. Krasniqi. Look at the Albanian version, page 2, paragraphs 2 and 3. Is that your statement? Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say there that the villages Brahim Batusha, Arbin Hajdari, Avni Hajdari, Jeton Hajdari and Melit Shehu were members of the KLA and that whenever they came into the village, they were wearing civilian clothing. Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, but it was in 2001, but in 1999 I didn't know that these were members of the KLA. In 2001, I saw them in KLA uniform. They came to the village, and it was at that time that I learned that they were members of the KLA, but before 1999 I did not know about them. After I returned to Kosova from Albania, it's then that I learned about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Could you tell me since I don't see these people on that list here - maybe I'm mistaken, at least I didn't see them on the list of the dead - do you know where they were on the 25th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I didn't know where they were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Could you tell me if you were aware at that time at all of the combat activities of the KLA against the Serb forces, police, and Serb civilians? Did you have any such knowledge at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I could listen on the radio or watch on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said yesterday that you stayed in the forest the whole day, in fact, until the following morning, and that those who had little children went to the house of Sejdi Batusha while you stayed in the forest. That's the statement of the 4th of April that you could see on the screen, and it's still in front of you. The next morning, the 25th of March, 1999, you say you saw Serb forces coming with all sorts of military vehicles, combat vehicles, and you described those vehicles. Could you just be more specific? Since you've already enumerated these vehicles, could you repeat that and tell us if you were able to see what colour the vehicles were; and since it was very early in the morning, it was still dark, you saw the lights on on the vehicles, were you able to see who was in the village that morning?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came, I could see the lights and that they stopped around the village. I don't know what colours they were because it was still dark, and then we went to the mountain, to the forest. I don't know about the colour. I couldn't see what colour they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about later that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 25th. On the 25th, I did not see any military machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Later on the 25th, there was no military machinery. Is that what you said? Maybe I misheard. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th, they were around the village and close to the road, and I couldn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's clearer now. Thank you. Mr. Krasniqi, tell me, please, you said yesterday that on the 26th of March, the tanks went up to the village, surrounded the village coming from the forest, and that not a single policeman went up to the forest where you were. You said they sent two men. One was Aziz Shehu - that's what you say - and the other's name is Sulejman Batusha. They came to tell everyone who was in the forest to return to the village. You also say that after that, you went to Sejdi Batusha's house, and you all gathered in his yard. Mr. Krasniqi, tell me about Aziz Shehu and Sulejman Batusha. Were those men who were pushed together with you into the house where the massacre took place?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is about the 26th, when the forces, the Serb military forces came to the forest above us in the mountain. That happened on the 26th of March, 1999. And then, they sent Sulejman Batusha and Aziz Shehu to take whoever had remained in the forest. We were gathered together in Sejdi Batusha's courtyard, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, about Aziz Shehu and Sulejman Batusha. Were they also executed on that occasion, during this event that we call a massacre here in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you about this small segment that is different here, so let's clarify it. Your statement that -- given to the investigators of the OTP on the 4th of April, 1999, in the English is D001-4180, paragraph 2, paragraph 5; the Albanian is D001-4926, paragraph 5, second sentence. You say in that statement: "At 9.00 on Friday," and you're referring to the 26th of March, "a group of about 15 policemen came into the forest where the refugees were hiding. I saw three Serb policemen who had white arm bands as they were giving instructions." Could you just clarify this for us. This group of 15 policemen who entered the forest in the morning, tell me, did they contact you, or did they send those two citizens that I referred to a few moments ago, Batusha and Hajdari, to tell you that you should leave the forest? I believe that this would be very important for the sake of the consistency of your statement to the very end.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policemen did not speak directly to me. They just sent Sulejman Batusha and Aziz Shehu to bring the people down to the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us clear up one more detail from your statement. On the 27th June, 2001, that's the date of the statement, the English version is D001-4129, page 2, paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply don't have the Albanian version. I have only the B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In that statement of the 27th of June -- can you tell us from the page in English that this is your signature? It's your statement to the ICTY of the 27th June, 2001. Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it here. No, it's not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We see written in capital letters in print, Mehmet Avdyli. Can I then conclude you didn't sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we're getting into an area where we are not clear. We have already discussion about the statement of the 27th of June, 2001. I believe what is before the witness is the statement of the 4th of April, 1999. So we need to have -- to get the right document before the witness, then have the witness answer clear questions in respect to what he is supposed to have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit I didn't hear what the Prosecutor has just said. If my learned friend, Mr. Stamp, could please repeat. I would like to know what kind of an objection you are making.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The objection is with respect to the clarity of the proceedings and the questions being asked, and it's not really an objection formally. I just want to assist. You are asking about -- counsel is asking about a statement of the 21st -- on the 27th of June, 2001, and referring to a document on the screen in e-court, which is not that statement but another statement. Counsel needs to get the document that he wants to ask about on e-court so that the witness could look at that, and then he could ask hopefully clear questions about whatever the witness is supposed to have said in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The short point you're putting, Mr. Stamp, is that questions are not being asked about the statement that is being displayed on the screen. There are two statements, one in 1999 and one in 2001, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, obviously I was not heard well, and that's why this confusion occurred. I asked for the statement of the witness of the 27th of June, 2001, to be shown to the witness. It was the statement given to the ICTY investigators, D001-429. That's the number. I also have the number of the B/C/S version, but I don't have the document in Albanian, at least not in e-court, but I will try to locate it with my assistant. It's D001-4209. That's the English version. And would you please let us look at that statement. Would you please show us page 2. We see the English and the B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I have a specific question. In that statement, when you were explaining what you were marking because there's a map attached to the statement, a map given to you by the investigator, you said: I wrote in 0900 on the 29 March, and that means that they took us out of Sejdi Batusha's house at 9.00 in the morning on the 29th of March, 1999, where men were separated from women and children. Which means that at 9 a.m., you were taken out of the house and men were separated from the women. That's what it says in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe there's a translation issue here again because the English translation I have is pretty much the same thing as his evidence. The English translation I have is: "We were moved out of the yard of Sejdi Batusha's house ..." That is, if I may, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 -- that's 6th paragraph down in the statement, and what the witness said in evidence is that they were put -- they were in the courtyard of Sejdi Batusha's house, and what we have here in the statement is that they were moved out of a yard. That is pretty much, it seems to me, consistent with what he said in evidence. And the short answer is that what I hear my friend saying, is that he said, the witness said he was moved out of the house. That is not what the statement says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The event happened, by the way, on the 26th the March. I think you'd mentioned the 29th once or twice, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. I wanted to show the Court the map marked by the witness, and I wanted to ask him about that; namely, I wanted to ask about the hour he wrote on the map and whether it is the correct hour. It's Exhibit P301 marked on page 22. That's what I read from the witness notification, and I'd like the map to be shown on the screen, so I can point that out to the witness and ask for clarification. This is the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is this map familiar to you, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This map was shown to me by the people from the Tribunal, the ones who took my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You see here 0900. That's the marking near the house of Sejdi Batusha. Do you see it, or do we need to zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What does that mean, 0900? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9.00 in the morning when we were taken out to the street, from the courtyard of Sejdi Batusha's house to the street, and there we were separated men from women and children. The women and children were told to go to Albania or go drown in the river Drin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So that's the meaning of this number, 0900?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Can you tell us today, who ordered you to line up three by three, and who told the women to go and drown or go to Albania with the children?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policemen in uniform, and they also had yellow and white bands on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you recognize the police officers? Were these people you knew?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
