utterances.text: Did you know the meaning of these yellow and white bands?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That occasion, did they take away your wallets, valuables, money?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took everything we had in our pockets - money, ID papers - and we had to hold our hands behind our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Tell me, how did the policemen do that in?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took the documents and the money out ourselves. Adem Asllani, they called him by name. He was about 60 years old, an elderly man, and they told him to collect everything together, make a pile at the feet of one policeman, and he went back to the place where he was lining up and put his hands behind his head again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, as for these uniformed men, were there any differences in the uniforms that they were wearing on that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what was the colour of the uniforms worn by the people who had yellow and white bands?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all dressed in dark blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the witness's statement displayed on the monitor, the one dated the 5th of October, 2001. The English version is D001-4218, page 2, please. And the Albanian version, D001-4226, but now it's page 3. In reference to the English version, I would like to draw everyone's attention to paragraphs 10, 11, 12, and 13 of page 2. As for the version in the Albanian language, I would like to draw your attention to page 3, paragraphs 2, 3, 4, 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The investigator asked you to describe the uniforms that you saw in Mala Krusa on the 26th of March, 1999, on or around that date, and then you said: "The first type of uniform," you are talking about the first type of uniform, you say "... is camouflage. They were paramilitaries, and they were wearing white ribbons on their arms. I did not see any insignia on their uniforms." "The second type of uniform I saw was a combination of green camouflage trousers and a plain green shirt." You say that you think that they could have been the Army of Yugoslavia, members of the Army of Yugoslavia? And the last third type -- well, you don't say that on the text, but I add this, you saw was the MUP blue camouflage uniform. These people were wearing yellow ribbons on their arms. Then you say, let me be more specific, that people from the MUP were wearing yellow ribbons and camouflage uniforms. Camouflage uniforms and white ribbons were worn by some other people. First of all, I'm going to ask you whether this is your statement, where this is described. Did you sign that? Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will admit that there are major differences between what you've been saying just now a few moments ago and what it was that you stated then. Tell me, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I did say that. I didn't know how to describe them exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, let me ask you briefly, then. Can we agree that your statement that you're looking at now is correct or, rather that, what you stated then was the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said in the statement is true. I have described in there everything that I saw with my own eyes, and I always speak the truth. I'm here to tell only the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to have these paragraphs from the statement in the English and Albanian language admitted into evidence. The reason is the major difference that exists between what the witness said today and what he said then. He did not refer to green uniforms at all. He only spoke of dark blue uniforms, and therefore I ask that this part of his statement be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll receive the whole statement, Mr. Djordjevic. It becomes very tricky if you look at only part of a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- and my friend keeps saying that there is a major difference. Of course, what's the difference is a matter for the Court to adjudicate upon eventually, but could I just point out that what he says in the statement is that: "I've been asked to describe the uniforms I saw in village on or about the 26th of March." What he was asked earlier in evidence was to describe the uniforms of the persons that were separating the women and the persons that were ordering them to the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I don't doubt what you're saying, but you will realise that that's the sort of thing that comes in submissions at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But -- [Overlapping speakers] submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. That statement will be received, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D0027, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like to ask to have this witness's statement displayed on the monitor, the one that he gave on the 7th of March, 2002. The English version is D001-4231, page 2, please. In Albanian, the number is D001 - that is Mr. Krasniqi's statement - /4237, again page 2. As for the English version, we are talking about paragraphs 3 and 4. As for the Albanian version, I'm referring to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, is this your statement, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to your transcript, the one that was just admitted into evidence, I would like to remind you here that you are making a correction in terms of paragraph 11, where you said that members of the paramilitary that you saw had yellow ribbons, so the paramilitaries had yellow ribbons. So you are excluding from the previous statement the part where you say blue camouflage uniform that was worn by members of the MUP. Now you say that these are paramilitaries, paramilitaries. On the left side of their chests and on their left arms. This is quite different from what we've heard until now because your statements to this date say that on their arms some had white ribbons, others had yellow ribbons, and now we see a member of the paramilitary you are describing who is wearing a white ribbon on his arm and a yellow ribbon on his chest. Could you please give us a comment, an explanation so that we would understand how come there is this difference and what this is all about, really?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they wore these bands on their arms. They know the reason why they wore those bands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, we are getting close to the end of our day's work. I can understand that you've lost your concentration a bit. This is hard work for all of us, but I have to repeat something that you obviously did not understand because you are obviously responding to something that I did not even ask you. In your statement that we see on the monitor here -- rather, do we see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber hasn't been able to find in this statement the passage that you are putting to the witness, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Page 2, paragraph 11. Over here, obviously -- just a moment, please. When one works, one is bound to make mistakes too. Obviously, I did not take this down right, so I will apologise. As for the page that we have here, I have a different set of questions. What I asked a few moments ago is something that I really did notice somewhere, where it is stated that there were yellow ribbons on the chest and white ribbons on the arm, but by the end of my cross, I hope that I will be able to find the exact references.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, what are you be profession at that point in time, on the 26th -- 25th of March, 1999? What was your line of work then?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agriculture. It was a farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As a farmer, are you aware of the difference -- are you aware of the difference between a house and a barn where cattle are kept?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know the difference. A house is a place where people live. Of course I know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that in the house that you were brought to, Rasim Batusha's house, there was hay that was supposed to be used for feeding animals. Did I misunderstand something? It is page 70 of the transcript, paragraphs 5 and 6, so that we have a clear reference what I'm referring to, paragraphs 5 and 6 on page 70. Could you please clarify this, as I assume that it must have been a mistake, but I would like to you tell us.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He bought that house as a structure, but he himself lived in another house. He kept the fodder for the animals in the first house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is quite clear. I'm going to go back to the first statement that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal on the 4th of April, 1999, when you said that this house was unfurnished and that no one lived there. So in view of what you are saying today, this seems to be a logical explanation. Now, the next thing I wish to ask you, it will have to do to your statement. Yesterday, it was the first time that you mentioned the two disabled persons were brought in, one you referred to from the very beginning of your testimony, and the other one you mentioned for the very first time only yesterday. What was the reason for not mentioning this other person in your first statements? I think that there have been five altogether up to now that you are testifying before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought I mentioned everything, but as you say we can make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see these two disabled persons from the room where you were, or, actually, before that, could you just describe to us once again, you said that there were two rooms. In which one of the two rooms were you so that we could understand better what it looked like and where it was in relation to the first room and, again, in relation to the door to the room that you were in.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the room on the right-hand side, the one that you go in from the road. It had two windows. I was in the far end corner. I was not near the window. On my right-hand side was Zenun Hajdari. He was close to the hay, close to the fodder for the animals that was there in the room where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May I infer, then, that this person, this disabled person was not at the door, the entrance door, that is, or close to the entrance door, because if I understand things correctly, you were in the other room that is farther away from the entrance door and that has two windows.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sait Hajdari, the disabled person in a wheelchair, he was at the entrance door to the corridor. I entered the room before them, but they didn't allow him to go in. They just left him there by the door. I personally proceeded to the room and went to the far end next to the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. You said yesterday that upon entering this room you experienced something terrible, that an execution started, that they started firing at you. You said that they were firing from machine guns through the window. You said that you did not know who it was that fired at you, but I wish to ask you the following. Before they started the fire, you said that they poured some liquid on you as you lay there in the blood of the man above you who had been hit by the fire. Tell me, by carefully studying the case, I realise that you did not mention a single time the pouring of this liquid. How can you explain that, that this is the first time you to refer this liquid and the fact that this is the first time that you mention the ear wounds that took longer to heal than the wounds on your hands? You did not mention something that important ever before your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think my friend first needs to establish from going through the various statements, whether or not the witness has mentioned that he had injuries to his ears, if that is what the question is about, and the pouring of the liquid because I do believe that the witness did mention that in his testimony before, that liquid was poured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point is this liquid was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is the mention now of liquid being poured onto the witness rather than a general use of liquid, if I understand Mr. Djordjevic correctly. Yes. Carry on, please, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll skip the injuries to the ear. I'm asking about the liquid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why hasn't it been mentioned until today?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they fired at us with their firearms, they poured this liquid in order to burn the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Krasniqi, and I think you understood it the first time, was why did you mention such an important detail for the first time only yesterday in your testimony? In the daily transcript, it was page 71, paragraph 12. Never in all of your statements did you mention that they poured some liquid to burn the bodies. Yesterday was the first time you mentioned it. Why did you never bring that up before?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've always mentioned this, and I'm sure that this is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have in my hand a transcript from his previous testimony in which he clearly says that they threw in a liquid into the room, so what my friend is putting to the witness, that he's saying this for the first time in evidence here yesterday, is not correct. That's the first thing. The second thing is that if there's also a point being made about the liquid being poured on him and not into the room, what he has said consistently yesterday is that liquid was poured into the room, and he said that about two or three times. So I'm -- the primary objection is that it is not correct by telling the witness that he has never said anything about liquid before, and I just ask for reference -- I just indicate to my friend that he could have a look at page 4374 of the transcript in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quite accept the intervention of my learned friend, Mr. Stamp. My question would then be why such an important detail does not feature in any of the previous statements of this witness given to the investigators. We can see when the statement was given in the Milutinovic case. I really did not see that passage. My omission, and I am guilty, but then let us stipulate that it was said in the Milutinovic case for the first time, and in no prior statement given to the Tribunal or any other organisation investigating the crime was it mentioned. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why wasn't it mentioned before that time in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every question that was made, I answered it telling the truth. It is more than true that this liquid was poured on the bodies. It didn't have any smell, but it was incendiary because it set the bodies on fire, and then they started to throw hay on the bodies and the maise stems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm going to ask you for the last time before I suggest that we take the break. Why was it the first time in the Milutinovic case that you mentioned the flammable liquid and never before? Give me any answer, and I'll be happy.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was asked about it, I gave the answer. So when I was asked about this detail, I provided them with the answer, and this is the liquid that caused my burns when I was in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose this is a good time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. I take it we will finish this witness today, including time for re-examination. Yes. We will adjourn now and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll continue from where I said that anyone who works makes mistakes sometimes. I gave a wrong exhibit number, and I'm sorry about that. I will do my best to finish this cross-examination today so that the witness should not have to stay in The Hague through the weekend. Now, may I ask for D001-4240 to be shown, in English language, page 2; and in Albanian, D001-4244. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, look at this Albanian language statement. Is this statement familiar to you? Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what to say. Maybe I have signed it. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly look at page 2 and the part of the statement where it says that you did, indeed, state that, and I'll ask you: Did you state that members of the paramilitary that you had seen had yellow bands on the left side of their chest and white arm bands on the right upper arm?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see them wearing ribbons or bands on their arms, but I can't remember whether -- which arm I said. Maybe I did, but now I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think it's possible that these soldiers whom you referred to as members of the paramilitary -- well, first of all, did you use the term "paramilitary" in that statement of the 7th of March, 2002?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't used the word "paramilitary."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is so, then Your Honours, I will not ask anymore questions on this subject. I'll just like to tender both these statements in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They'll be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That'll be D00028, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, tell me, who are Slavisa Petkovic and Ljubisa Stankovic? First of all, do you know these people, and if you do, tell me who they are.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are Serbs from our village. They were born and grew up in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, did you remember ever stating that these two persons were in civilian clothes and that they were the ones who covered the bodies with corn husks, that they were not wearing police uniforms, that they were in civilian clothes. Do you remember ever saying that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now what I said then, but I can tell you now that I saw them when they were throwing corn husks on the people -- on the bodies of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell me if they were the only ones doing that, throwing corn husks on the bodies, or were there some other people doing the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw those two at that moment, only those two I saw when I was at my uncle's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Were they wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now whether they were in civilian clothes or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this way: Did you ever see these two people in police uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now at that moment what kind of clothes they were wearing. I just saw them carrying the maise stems. However, I can't remember now what they were dressed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility, then, in your statement of the 7th of March, 2002, you said that they were in fact two Serb civilians engaged in that activity? Do you think that's possible?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it then and I'm saying it now, that it was those two, but I can't remember what kinds of clothes they were wearing. Now I can't remember even what I said at the time about the clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Tell me, you said today before this Court that Refki Rashkaj and Jeton Shehu were seen by you running when you left your uncle's house that evening. Did you say that they are actually survivors, that they were not victims of the massacre you are telling us about?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them in the forest, close to the stream. They were not killed in the massacre, but when they had tried to escape. I did not see them in the beginning, but when I was trying to leave, I saw them, that they had been killed there in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that yesterday for the first time, or did you mention that in your prior statements or in the testimony in the Milutinovic case, concerning Refki Rashkaj and Adnan Shehu. You did mention them before, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I mentioned it when I testified the other times, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell me, Mr. Krasniqi, are you able to tell the Court today whether Adnan Shehu and Refki Rashkaj were killed and, if so, how they were killed, or did they have a different fate? I want to clear that up, and whatever you say, please tell us how you know what you know.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they were killed because I did not see them when they were killed. I just saw them dead. When we were in those two rooms and the corridor, I know that they were inside, but I don't know how they got out, how they fled. When I got out myself, I thought that I was the only one who had survived the massacre, and everybody else had perished. There were no other survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you agree with me that you saw them killed on the 26th of March, 1999, as you say?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why, to the investigators of the ICTY and the international organisations that questioned you, you said nothing about these events and you didn't mention them until yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did mention them. I know that they had been killed. I don't think that what you said is true, that I did not mention them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, be so kind as to answer another question. Yesterday, when you were speaking of events in Nogavac, it's page 76 of yesterday's transcript, pages 19, 20, and so on, you said the Serbs took your money and told you to stay in the village until further notice, until you move on to Albania. It seems to me that's another thing you mentioned for the first time yesterday. You had not spoken before that about the events in Nogavac and these particular details; correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said is accurate. I was in Nogavac. About the money that had been taken from the people, this is what I heard from other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The only thing that worries me and concerns me is that you never mentioned that before until yesterday. You also said that the people who were going from Kosovo to Albania had their money taken away from them at the border crossing and that they had to throw their passports onto a pile. That's also in yesterday's transcript. All that I had occasion to study, all the evidence that I had from you in this case and in others, doesn't feature any reference to this, not until yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I don't want to say I'm certain, but I don't think what counsel is putting to the witness again is correct, that the witness never said these things before. I do believe that in the mass -- in the Milutinovic trial, and also in a previous statement the witness has mentioned that persons were -- that property was taken from people at the border. I'll try to find the references.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, when you described the event on the border crossing when they kept you tied to the radiator --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for the statement of the 4th of April, 1999, to be shown again, D001-4180, and Albanian, D001-4196.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You did not mention the two members of the KLA from Retimlje yesterday. Can you tell us very briefly about this? I read that in your statement. Can you just clarify, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people from Retija [phoen] were not from the KLA. They were wearing civilian clothes. They were inside that border crossing point where I was taken. I was tied up. I don't know anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding the injuries you sustained as you were escaping the -- from the execution site, did you receive any treatment in Albania from a physician, because you said you had burns.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Kukes. I just received some treatment there. People were coming in droves, and they needed help. I left and as I said, I used alternative medication, bear fat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any medical documentation from the time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, no documentation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, from the statement of the 4th of April, we see a large number of names with their age and details about families, their full names, their age, et cetera. Can you tell us briefly how in the situation that prevailed then you managed to compile such a complete list with so many details?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's yesterday's transcript page 70, paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm asking you this because in response to the Prosecution on the subject, you answered: I did not count them then, and I don't count them now because that causes me pain. I understand your pain, but what does it mean, that you didn't count them then and you are not counting them now, although we have a list of 100 persons, which the Prosecution says you drew up.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from the Tribunal, when they took my statement, they asked me for the names. I knew how many people entered the location where the massacre occurred, and I mentioned the names of those people. I had burns. I was traumatised. I was scared. However, I did mention the names, and they took them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Because of the circumstances that prevailed, I'm surprised by the completeness and precision you displayed in compiling this list and also by the power of your memory. That's why I'm asking, did you draw up the list alone or together with some other people?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody from the village, from my village was there. God help me, these people are still missing. There are mothers left without sons and without male members of the family. These people have perished. We don't know where their remains are, and you might well know where the people from Serbia took these bodies to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you if anybody helped you compile the list. I didn't mean only the men. I meant perhaps the wives and mothers that you were with at the time. That's all I meant.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of April, I hadn't met anyone from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be able to enumerate all the villages today before the Court, to tell us everybody's age, and list all the households and families in the village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even to this day, I cannot count all of them. I wouldn't be able to mention all the names. I don't feel well to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer another question for me, the same transcript. I am sorry about this, Mr. Krasniqi, seriously. I have one more question to put to you. It has to do with your same statement of the 4th of April. You say in your statement: Now I'm a refugee in Albania, and I was chosen to make this statement for the ICTY. Who was it that chose you to make this statement for the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute, please. Perhaps there's a translation issue here, but I think we should refer to the precise language used in the signed document before the Court because that is at odds with all what my friend just read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The word has been translated in English as "elected" rather than "chosen." If there's a difference which is relevant, I'm not sure what it is, but your point is, Were you chosen or elected by somebody; if so, who? I think you should proceed with that question, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may respectfully, Your Honour, I think what was quoted to the witness was that he had -- that he was chosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Chosen rather than elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but used in the context that he was chosen by someone else. He was chosen. He is saying in his statement that he himself elected or chose to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see now the distinction you make, Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- which I didn't earlier. I'm sorry. Have you follow that, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Indeed. Indeed. It has to do with the translation into B/C/S that is part of the OTP documentation, also because of the translation into Albanian. That's why I put this question. This error should not remain an error as such. That is why I'm asking the witness to say what Mr. Stamp said just now, if that is the case. It's not that I doubt anything, but I would just like to finish my cross-examination as soon as possible, but I would like to hear directly from the witness, and this is really one of the difficulties involved in these proceedings, among others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I think the essence of what's being asked of you is, Did you yourself volunteer to come forward and make a statement, or did someone else or some other people push you forward to give the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wasn't pushed by anyone into giving this statement. I wasn't chosen or elected by anyone. This was my statement. I still have the marks on my hands. The person who was on top of me, his blood was still on me to the day I went to Kukes. I still have clothes that have been burnt, but I didn't want these people to die in vain, and that's where I got my will from. I wanted people to hear about that. To this day, we still don't know where the bodies of these victims are, the bodies of these men who were burnt to ashes. This was the only driving force for me to come here to the Tribunal and tell the truth. To this days, it's not easy for me, believe me. I don't feel good when I speak about all these men who died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Krasniqi. Is there something further, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what I wish to do, as well, to thank the witness. That is what I thought the situation was, but I felt that this had to be corrected because this is a bad mistake in the translation, and I think that it could lead to a lot of confusion during the proceedings, so I think it's best dealt with right now. Before I complete my cross-examination now today, I would just like to clarify another thing that I heard today and did not find very clear. I heard from the witness say today that 20 bodies were identified, and he says: I never found out where the others were. Did I hear this right, or is this a mistake? I heard that today as his words during the direct examination carried out by my learned friend, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to the remaining bodies, that we don't know, where they are. The Serbs only know where their remains, their ashes were taken to once they cleaned the location of the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about these 20 identified bodies that the witness is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is this all about, Mr. Krasniqi? I'm asking you, actually.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some remains were found. They were identified. This is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you to tell us who it was that identified these mortal remains, and where were they found, actually, because this is the first time we hear of this, and it is very important.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who identified the remains and where these remains were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us since your memory remains intact as to the persons who were killed during this massacre, who were the persons that were among these 20? I would suggest that you even be allowed to use your statement from the 6th of April, 1999, so that we would know who the persons identified were and whose mortal remains were found. You didn't tell us, though, where they were found and who identified them, but obviously, that was the case. We see that, too, because to this day the OTP never provided information, a single case about 20 identified citizens of Mala Krusa after the massacre that took place on the 26th of March, 1999. Can you do that now, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot help you as to who identified the remains and where these remains were found. This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, just one more question. As for Dmitrije Nikolic, your neighbor, you kept saying yesterday when you spoke about him that you saw him in police uniform, that the policemen gathered at his place. Tell me, what was he by profession, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in a wine cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, tell me, did he have a kind of cafe or coffee bar or some kind of a catering facility in his house where citizens gathered before, as well, the citizens of Mala Krusa, that is.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People came to this cafe that he opened, the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence could put a large number of questions to this witness, and I have them noted down here. However, what we heard from this witness today will suffice for the Defence case that will be developed as we go along, and I'm going to thank Mr. Krasniqi today for having testified today, for having come to this court to enable us to get as much information as possible to the best of his ability, and with those remarks I would like to end my cross-examination of Mr. Krasniqi today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Is there any re-examination, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a couple questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were asked today about the houses that were set on fire while you were in the forest and otherwise. You said you don't know how they were set on fire, but you saw smoke coming from the village. Can you just tell us, what were -- what was the condition of the Albanian houses as you saw when you returned to your village in July or June 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came back from Albania to Kosova, the houses were destroyed, burned down. They were turned to ashes. The state was miserable. Only there were some walls still standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown a document which became D27, and that is your statement of the 5th of October, 2001, I think - yes - in which you described three types of uniforms that you saw -- according to this document you say that you saw in Krusha e Vogel on or about the 26th of March, 1999. Earlier, I had asked you about the uniforms of the persons who were involved in separating the women from the men and ushering you into the house or the barn where the executions took place, and you said that these were -- those persons who did that were in blue police uniforms. What I'd like to ask you is this: Where did you see the persons who were wearing the green camouflage uniforms and the combination of green camouflage trousers and plain green shirt that is referred to in your statement of October 2001? Where did you see these persons in the various types of green uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were on the road, standing on the sides of the road while we were there on the road with our hands on our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly, if you could look at the statement, and this is -- this had become Exhibit P305, but I think you have it in front of you, the list. If you could look back at the list, please, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could bring up --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in answer to the question from my learned friend that Aziz Shehu was also executed in the house. If you look at the last page of the list, or in English it's the penultimate page, and I think it's probably the penultimate page in Albanian as well. Can you look on your list there for where you have listed the people from the Shehu family. You will see third from last on the list Haziz, age 42. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that the Haziz Shehu that you said was also killed in execution?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just have a moment to consult with my colleagues, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was suggested to you in the course of cross-examination that you didn't say anything about your ear being burnt, and we showed, I think, a video in which you were showing the burn injury to your ear and to the side of your head. Who told the investigator at that time about the injury, the burn injury to your ear? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, but I have to react. We did not hear any interpretation where the witness explains that his ear was injured. We just saw the picture, part of the video-clip where his injured ear is shown, and I would appreciate it very much if my learned friend did not ask this question. The witness didn't definitely not say, My ear is hurt. We just saw the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that we saw the picture, but I'm just asking the person -- the witness, sorry, how is it that the investigators knew that his ear was to be focussed upon, that his ear was burnt during the incident of the execution, and the witness has answered anyway that he was the person that told them about it, and that is why they did the video. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Krasniqi, you'll be pleased to know that that completes the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the help you've been able to give us and the way you have been able to answer the questions that were put to you. We're grateful for what you have done, and now the court officers will show you from the courtroom and make other arrangements in due course for you to return to your home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you have that look of expectation on your face.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may just mention one thing with your leave, I had promised earlier with respect to P305 to give an accurate count as to the amount of names that are on that list. I must confess that I needed to confirm because every time I myself counted it, I got a different number varying between 102 and 104. It has now been counted by someone who is much more capable of counting than I am, a better counter, and there are 103 names on the list. And according to the evidence, three of those persons were not in the room; that is, Sefer Batusha and Muharrem Batusha's nephew, and also son of Sinan Shehu, and also according to the testimony, Lufti Ramadani and Qamil Shehu were in the room but survived. And these are the persons on the list. So it's 103 minus 5. I hope I have done what I indicated I would do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You will be supported in that respect by the count made by the Judges, and we, too reach 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. I was the only person mistaken, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So with that comforting reassurance that we have got the number correct, we will adjourn now and continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of February, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
